What options do I have for publishing my Obsidian vault as a web application?

Primary pick: QuartzMD (Quartz 4) — SSG built for Obsidian vaults (wikilinks, backlinks, graph, search, popover previews). Official GitHub Pages path: fork/create a Quartz repo, point it at your vault content, add the deploy.yml workflow from Quartz hosting — GitHub Pages, set repo Pages → Source: GitHub Actions, set baseUrl in quartz.config.ts to your https://<user>.github.io/<repo>/ URL, then publish with npx quartz sync after edits. Requires Node v22+ and npm.

2. Commit; enable GitHub Actions Pages deploy (workflow builds with npx quartz build, uploads public/).

3. Keep editing in Obsidian; sync vault into the Quartz content directory (or use a separate content repo/submodule—many gardens symlink or copy content/).

4. Push to the v4 branch (or whatever your workflow targets); site updates automatically.

Alternative on GitHub Pages: Digital Garden plugin — if you want selective publish from inside Obsidian (dg-publish: true per note) rather than building the whole vault, install oleeskild/obsidian-digital-garden, push to a GitHub repo, deploy gh-pages (or the plugin’s documented GitHub Pages flow). Less “full SSG control,” more “mark notes public in Obsidian.”
GitHub Pages + Obsidian-native static site (recommended stack)

What to skip for this goal — raw markdown on Pages without an SSG (broken wikilinks); Hugo/MkDocs unless you already run an export pipeline (more glue than Quartz for Obsidian-first gardens). Obsidian Publish is not GitHub Pages.
GitHub Pages + Obsidian-native static site (recommended stack)

Caveats — Community plugins (Dataview, Canvas, etc.) still do not execute on the static site; Quartz documents a trailing-slash quirk on GitHub Pages vs Cloudflare if you care about old URLs (hosting note).

What's the fastest way to create a new page according to a template in Obsidian? Is there a keyboard shortcut?

Short answer: The core Templates plugin does not create a brand-new note from a template—it only inserts template text into the active note. Obsidian ships no default hotkey for template commands; you assign one under Settings → Hotkeys. For fastest “new file + template content”, use a community workflow (QuickAdd Template choice or Templater folder/trigger templates) and bind that command to a shortcut.

What's the fastest way to create a new page according to a template in Obsidian? Is there a keyboard shortcut?

Enable Settings → Core plugins → Templates, set Template folder location, then run Templates: Insert template (ribbon Insert template, or Command palette). Optional related commands: Templates: Insert current date, Templates: Insert current time.

Keyboard shortcut: none by default. Search Templates: Insert template in Settings → Hotkeys, click +, press your combo (many people use something like Ctrl+Alt+T / Cmd+Option+T—pick one that does not conflict).

Two-step “new page” with core only: File: Create new note (Ctrl+N / Cmd+N), then your Templates: Insert template hotkey or palette command—works but is slower than a single “create from template” command.

QuickAdd — add a Template choice (template path + target folder), run QuickAdd: Run QuickAdd once to verify, then in Hotkeys bind the choice’s command (e.g. QuickAdd: <your choice name>) to one key. One shortcut → new file in the right folder with template applied.
Fastest general “new note from this template” (community)

Templater — for automation beyond plain insertion: Folder templates (auto-apply when creating in a folder), Trigger Templater on new file creation, and/or add templates to Templater’s hotkey list so Templater: <template> is bindable.
Fastest general “new note from this template” (community)

Net: Yes, you can use a keyboard shortcut, but you (or a plugin) must assign it—except where Daily notes / Unique note creator already apply a configured template as part of their own “create note” commands.

Planned obsolescence = intentionally shortening a product’s useful life (or making it feel outdated sooner) to encourage replacement and repeat sales. (Wikipedia)

1932 (named explicitly): Bernard London’s pamphlet Ending the Depression Through Planned Obsolescence argued that shortening product lifetimes could stimulate economic demand during the Great Depression. (Wikimedia Commons)

1925–1939 (often-cited early example): The Phoebus cartel in incandescent lightbulbs is widely cited as an industrial case where lifespan was standardized downward (often to ~1,000 hours), making it a classic planned-obsolescence story. (Wikipedia)

1954 (popularized in design/marketing): Industrial designer Brooks Stevens framed planned obsolescence as “instilling in the buyer the desire to own something a little newer, a little better, a little sooner than is necessary.” (Industrial Designers Society of America)
Late 1950s–1960s (turns into critique): Public backlash grew, and planned obsolescence became linked to “throwaway” consumer culture and manipulation-by-marketing critiques. (daily.jstor.org)
